claim: Anterior pituitary hormones, traditionally thought to have unitary functions in regulating single endocrine targets, act on multiple somatic tissues, such as bone, fat, and liver.
source: There is increasing evidence that anterior pituitary hormones, traditionally thought to have unitary functions in regulating single endocrine targets, act on multiple somatic tissues, such as bone, fat, and liver.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing these actions.

claim: There is emerging evidence for anterior pituitary hormone action on brain receptors in mediating central neural and peripheral somatic functions.
source: There is also emerging evidence for anterior pituitary hormone action on brain receptors in mediating central neural and peripheral somatic functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the literature review and citations provided in the manuscript.

claim: Tshr is expressed in 173 brain regions, nuclei and subnuclei.
source: We have used RNAscope, a technology that allows the detection of mRNA at single-transcript level, together with protein level validation, to document Tshr expression in 173 and Fshr expression in 353 brain regions, nuclei and subnuclei identified using the Atlas for the Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fshr is expressed in 353 brain regions, nuclei and subnuclei.
source: We have used RNAscope, a technology that allows the detection of mRNA at single-transcript level, together with protein level validation, to document Tshr expression in 173 and Fshr expression in 353 brain regions, nuclei and subnuclei identified using the Atlas for the Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lhcgr transcripts are identified in 401 brain regions, nuclei and subnuclei.
source: We also identified Lhcgr transcripts in 401 brain regions, nuclei and subnuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FSHR transcripts are co-localized in MALAT1-positive neurons in human brain samples.
source: Complementarily, we used ViewRNA, another single-transcript detection technology, to establish the expression of FSHR in human brain samples, where transcripts were co-localized in MALAT1-positive neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by ViewRNA data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All three receptors (TSHR, LHCGR, FSHR) show high expression in the ventricular region.
source: In addition, we show high expression for all three receptors in the ventricular region—with yet unknown functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data showing transcript densities in ventricular regions.

claim: Tshr expression in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle is similar to that of thyroid follicular cells.
source: Intriguingly, Tshr and Fshr expression in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle was similar to that of the thyroid follicular cells and testicular Sertoli cells, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative RNAscope data between brain and peripheral tissues.

claim: Fshr expression in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle is similar to that of testicular Sertoli cells.
source: Intriguingly, Tshr and Fshr expression in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle was similar to that of the thyroid follicular cells and testicular Sertoli cells, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative RNAscope data between brain and peripheral tissues.

claim: Fshr is localized to NeuN-positive neurons in the granular layer of the dentate gyrus in murine brain.
source: In contrast, Fshr was localized to NeuN-positive neurons in the granular layer of the dentate gyrus in murine and human brain—both are Alzheimer's disease-vulnerable regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-localization with NeuN.

claim: Fshr is localized to NeuN-positive neurons in the granular layer of the dentate gyrus in human brain.
source: In contrast, Fshr was localized to NeuN-positive neurons in the granular layer of the dentate gyrus in murine and human brain—both are Alzheimer's disease-vulnerable regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by ViewRNA data in human brain samples.

claim: The granular layer of the dentate gyrus is an Alzheimer's disease-vulnerable region.
source: In contrast, Fshr was localized to NeuN-positive neurons in the granular layer of the dentate gyrus in murine and human brain—both are Alzheimer's disease-vulnerable regions.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Alzheimer's disease pathology.

claim: TSH receptor (TSHR) haploinsufficiency causes profound bone loss in mice.
source: We established, for the first time, a direct action of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) on bone and found that TSH receptor (TSHR) haploinsufficiency causes profound bone loss in mice (Abe et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) displays direct effects on the skeleton to cause bone loss.
source: We also found that follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), hitherto thought to solely regulate gonadal function, displayed direct effects on the skeleton to cause bone loss (Sun et al., 2006), and on fat cells, to cause adipogenesis and body fat accumulation (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: FSH displays direct effects on fat cells to cause adipogenesis and body fat accumulation.
source: We also found that follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), hitherto thought to solely regulate gonadal function, displayed direct effects on the skeleton to cause bone loss (Sun et al., 2006), and on fat cells, to cause adipogenesis and body fat accumulation (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Oxytocin and vasopressin display direct, but opposing, skeletal actions.
source: Likewise, we showed that hormones from the posterior pituitary, namely, oxytocin and vasopressin, displayed direct, but opposing, skeletal actions—effects that may relate to the pathogenesis of bone loss in pregnancy and lactation, and in chronic hyponatremia, respectively (Sun et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2016; Tamma et al., 2009; Tamma et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: A TSHβ variant (TSHβv) is expressed in bone marrow macrophages.
source: We find the expression of a TSHβ variant (TSHβv) in bone marrow macrophages, while oxytocin is expressed by both osteoblasts and osteoclasts (Colaianni et al., 2011; Colaianni et al., 2012; Baliram et al., 2013; Baliram et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Oxytocin is expressed by both osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
source: We find the expression of a TSHβ variant (TSHβv) in bone marrow macrophages, while oxytocin is expressed by both osteoblasts and osteoclasts (Colaianni et al., 2011; Colaianni et al., 2012; Baliram et al., 2013; Baliram et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Oxytocin receptors are expressed in various brain regions and function in regulating peripheral actions, such as social behavior and satiety.
source: There is a compelling body of literature to support the expression of oxytocin receptors in various brain regions, and their function in regulating peripheral actions, such as social behavior and satiety (Sun et al., 2019; Bale et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: There is relatively scant information on the expression and function of the anterior pituitary glycoprotein hormone family of receptors (FSHR, TSHR, and LHCGR) in the brain.
source: However, there is relatively scant information on the expression and, importantly, function of the anterior pituitary glycoprotein hormone family of receptors, namely, FSHR, TSHR, and luteinizing hormone/human chorionic gonadotropin receptor (LHCGR).
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature.

claim: Discrete sites of the rat, mouse, and human brain express receptors for FSHR, TSHR, and LHCGR.
source: Discrete sites of the rat, mouse, and human brain express receptors for these hormones, with several studies pointing to their relationship to neural functions, such as cognition, learning, neuronal plasticity, and sensory perception, as well as to neuropsychiatric disorders, including affective disorders and neurodegeneration (Crisanti et al., 2001; Emanuele et al., 1985; Lei et al., 1993; Luan et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2020; Blair et al., 2019; Apaja et al., 2004; Naicker and Naidoo, 2018; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work and Table 1.

claim: Brain glycoprotein hormone receptors are related to neural functions such as cognition, learning, neuronal plasticity, and sensory perception.
source: Discrete sites of the rat, mouse, and human brain express receptors for these hormones, with several studies pointing to their relationship to neural functions, such as cognition, learning, neuronal plasticity, and sensory perception, as well as to neuropsychiatric disorders, including affective disorders and neurodegeneration (Crisanti et al., 2001; Emanuele et al., 1985; Lei et al., 1993; Luan et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2020; Blair et al., 2019; Apaja et al., 2004; Naicker and Naidoo, 2018; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work and Table 1.

claim: Brain glycoprotein hormone receptors are related to neuropsychiatric disorders, including affective disorders and neurodegeneration.
source: Discrete sites of the rat, mouse, and human brain express receptors for these hormones, with several studies pointing to their relationship to neural functions, such as cognition, learning, neuronal plasticity, and sensory perception, as well as to neuropsychiatric disorders, including affective disorders and neurodegeneration (Crisanti et al., 2001; Emanuele et al., 1985; Lei et al., 1993; Luan et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2020; Blair et al., 2019; Apaja et al., 2004; Naicker and Naidoo, 2018; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work and Table 1.

claim: RNAscope uses ~20 pairs of transcript-specific double Z-probes to hybridize 10-µm-thick whole-brain sections.
source: RNAscope, which allows the detection of single transcripts, uses ~20 pairs of transcript-specific double Z-probes to hybridize 10-µm-thick whole-brain sections.
evidence: This claim describes the technical methodology used in the study.

claim: Tshr was detected bilaterally in 173 brain nuclei and subnuclei.
source: Tshr was detected bilaterally in 173 brain nuclei and subnuclei, in the following descending order of transcript densities: ventricular region, olfactory bulb, forebrain, hypothalamus, medulla, cerebellum, midbrain and pons, cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Tshr transcript density is highest in the ventricular region, followed by olfactory bulb, forebrain, hypothalamus, medulla, cerebellum, midbrain and pons, cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus.
source: Tshr was detected bilaterally in 173 brain nuclei and subnuclei, in the following descending order of transcript densities: ventricular region, olfactory bulb, forebrain, hypothalamus, medulla, cerebellum, midbrain and pons, cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Thyroid glands from Tshr–/– mice do not show a Tshr RNAscope signal, proving probe specificity.
source: Importantly, thyroid glands from Tshr–/– mice did not show a signal, proving probe specificity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tshr expression in pooled brain samples was confirmed by qPCR.
source: Tshr expression in pooled brain samples was confirmed by qPCR (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The hypothalamus and hippocampus express Tshr, with hypothalamic expression being considerably higher (p<0.01) in females than in males.
source: The hypothalamus and hippocampus expressed Tshr, with hypothalamic expression being considerably higher (p<0.01) in females than in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing sex differences in Tshr expression.

claim: The ependymal layer of the third ventricle has the highest Tshr transcript density among brain regions.
source: Furthermore, within other regions of the brain, highest Tshr densities were as follows: ependymal layer of the third ventricle (slightly higher than the thyroid follicular cells); VTT in the olfactory bulb; HDB in the forebrain; MTu in the hypothalamus; SoIV in the medulla; PFI in the cerebellum; LDTg in midbrain and pons; DP in the cerebral cortex; DG in hippocampus; and PPT in the thalamus (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1; see Appendix 1 for nomenclature).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Tshr transcript density in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle is slightly higher than in thyroid follicular cells.
source: Furthermore, within other regions of the brain, highest Tshr densities were as follows: ependymal layer of the third ventricle (slightly higher than the thyroid follicular cells); VTT in the olfactory bulb; HDB in the forebrain; MTu in the hypothalamus; SoIV in the medulla; PFI in the cerebellum; LDTg in midbrain and pons; DP in the cerebral cortex; DG in hippocampus; and PPT in the thalamus (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1; see Appendix 1 for nomenclature).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative RNAscope data in Figure 1D.

claim: Abundant GFP immunofluorescence was detected in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle in Tshr+/– heterozygous mice.
source: Consistent with our RNAscope finding, profound GFP-ir was noted in the ependymal region of the third ventricle, mostly in NeuN-negative cells, but with some neuronal localization (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: GFP immunofluorescence in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle is mostly in NeuN-negative cells, but with some neuronal localization.
source: Consistent with our RNAscope finding, profound GFP-ir was noted in the ependymal region of the third ventricle, mostly in NeuN-negative cells, but with some neuronal localization (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The SVZ of the lateral ventricles, and the SI, and dorsal and ventral BNST of the forebrain show GFP immunoreactivity in Tshr+/– mice.
source: The SVZ of the lateral ventricles, and the SI, and dorsal and ventral BNST of the forebrain also showed GFP-ir, but immunoreactivity was much lower than the ependymal layer of the third ventricle (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GFP immunoreactivity in the SVZ, SI, and BNST is much lower than in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle.
source: The SVZ of the lateral ventricles, and the SI, and dorsal and ventral BNST of the forebrain also showed GFP-ir, but immunoreactivity was much lower than the ependymal layer of the third ventricle (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Lhcgr expression was documented in 401 brain nuclei and subnuclei.
source: Thus, we mapped Lhcgr in mouse brain to document expression in 401 brain nuclei and subnuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lhcgr RNAscope probe specificity was established by a positive signal in testicular Leydig cells and an absent signal in juxtaposed Sertoli cells.
source: Probe specificity was established by a positive signal in testicular Leydig cells, and with an absent signal in juxtaposed Sertoli cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by control data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ventricular regions display the highest Lhcgr transcript density.
source: Notably similar to Tshr transcripts, the ventricular regions displayed the highest transcript density (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: FSHR is expressed in mouse, rat, and human brains, particularly in AD-vulnerable regions, including hippocampus and cortex.
source: We recently reported the expression of FSHR in mouse, rat, and human brains, particularly in AD-vulnerable regions, including hippocampus and cortex (Xiong et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: FSH exacerbates AD-like neuropathology and cognitive decline in 3xTg, APP/PS1, and APP-KI mice.
source: We also found that FSH exacerbated AD-like neuropathology and cognitive decline in 3xTg, APP/PS1, and APP-KI mice, while the inhibition of FSH action rescued this phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Inhibition of FSH action rescues AD-like neuropathology and cognitive decline in 3xTg, APP/PS1, and APP-KI mice.
source: We also found that FSH exacerbated AD-like neuropathology and cognitive decline in 3xTg, APP/PS1, and APP-KI mice, while the inhibition of FSH action rescued this phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of Fshr in the hippocampus prevents the onset of AD-like features.
source: Most notably, shRNA-mediated knockdown of the Fshr in the hippocampus prevented the onset of AD-like features (Xiong et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Fshr is expressed at single-transcript resolution in 353 brain nuclei and subnuclei.
source: Here, using RNAscope, we report the expression of Fshr at the single-transcript resolution in 353 brain nuclei and subnuclei—and suggest that FSHR in the brain may have roles beyond cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FSHR in the brain may have roles beyond cognition.
source: Here, using RNAscope, we report the expression of Fshr at the single-transcript resolution in 353 brain nuclei and subnuclei—and suggest that FSHR in the brain may have roles beyond cognition.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the widespread expression of Fshr in multiple brain regions.

claim: Fshr RNAscope probe specificity was established by a positive signal in testicular Sertoli cells and an absent signal in juxtaposed Leydig cells.
source: Probe specificity was established by a positive signal in testicular Sertoli cells, and an absent signal in juxtaposed Leydig cells and in the testes of Fshr–/– mice—as negative controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by control data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fshr RNAscope probe specificity was established by an absent signal in the testes of Fshr–/– mice.
source: Probe specificity was established by a positive signal in testicular Sertoli cells, and an absent signal in juxtaposed Leydig cells and in the testes of Fshr–/– mice—as negative controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FSHR is expressed in NeuN-positive neurons.
source: Immunofluorescence confirmed the expression of FSHR in NeuN-positive neurons, but not in GFAP-positive glial cells or IBA1-positive microglia (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FSHR is not expressed in GFAP-positive glial cells.
source: Immunofluorescence confirmed the expression of FSHR in NeuN-positive neurons, but not in GFAP-positive glial cells or IBA1-positive microglia (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FSHR is not expressed in IBA1-positive microglia.
source: Immunofluorescence confirmed the expression of FSHR in NeuN-positive neurons, but not in GFAP-positive glial cells or IBA1-positive microglia (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fshr transcript density is highest in the ventricular region, followed by cerebellum, olfactory bulb, hippocampus, cerebral cortex, medulla, midbrain and pons, forebrain, thalamus, and hypothalamus.
source: Fshr transcript density was highest in the ventricular region, followed, in descending order, by the cerebellum, olfactory bulb, hippocampus, cerebral cortex, medulla, midbrain and pons, forebrain, thalamus, and hypothalamus (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Fshr transcript density in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle is slightly higher than in testicular Sertoli cells.
source: Within each region, respectively, the highest transcript densities were as follows: ependymal layer of the third ventricle (slightly higher than the testicular Sertoli cells); PFI in the cerebellum; GrA in the olfactory bulb; GrDG in the hippocampus; AIV in the cerebral cortex; RMg in the medulla; MHb in the thalamus; IPDL in midbrain and pons; aci in the forebrain; and ArcL in the hypothalamus (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative RNAscope data in Figure 3D.

claim: FSHR expression is noted in neuronal cells co-expressing the noncoding RNA MALAT1 in the granular layer of the dentate gyrus in human brain.
source: Expression was noted in neuronal cells co-expressing the noncoding RNA MALAT1 in the GrDG—consistent with the RNAscope data in mouse brain—and in the parahippocampal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by ViewRNA data in human brain samples.

claim: FSHR expression is noted in the parahippocampal cortex in human brain.
source: Expression was noted in neuronal cells co-expressing the noncoding RNA MALAT1 in the GrDG—consistent with the RNAscope data in mouse brain—and in the parahippocampal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by ViewRNA data in human brain samples.

claim: FSHR is expressed in a population of excitatory glutamatergic neurons in human brain.
source: This latter data is consistent with FSHR expression in a population of excitatory glutamatergic neurons noted in human brain by 10× single-cell RNA-seq (Allen Brain Atlas).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data from the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: FSHR is expressed in the frontal, cingulate, temporal, parietal, and occipital subregions of human cortex in postmortem normal and AD brains.
source: Affymetrix microarray analysis confirmed FSHR expression in the frontal, cingulate, temporal, parietal, and occipital subregions of human cortex in postmortem normal and AD brains (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Affymetrix microarray data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FSHR expression trends to be higher in the frontal cortex of AD brains compared to unaffected brains (p=0.060).
source: Interestingly, FSHR expression trended to be higher in the frontal cortex of the AD brains compared to that of unaffected brains (p=0.060).
evidence: This claim is supported by Affymetrix microarray data showing a trend toward significance.

claim: Brain FSHR may have a wider role in central regulation beyond cognition.
source: In all, the data suggest that, beyond a primary role in regulating cognition, brain FSHR may have a wider role in the central regulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the widespread expression of FSHR in multiple brain regions.

claim: Tshr, Lhcgr, and Fshr are expressed in multiple brain regions.
source: We report here for the first time that Tshr, Lhcgr, and Fshr are expressed in multiple brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: There is a surprising and striking overlap in central neural distribution of TSHR, LHCGR, and FSHR, with highest transcript densities in the ventricular regions.
source: Specifically, we find a surprising and striking overlap in central neural distribution of the three receptors—with highest transcript densities in the ventricular regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data showing similar distribution patterns for all three receptors.

claim: TSHR and FSHR expression levels in the ependymal layer of the third ventricle are similar to those of thyroid follicular cells and testicular Sertoli cells, respectively, suggesting a primary role for these receptors in central neural regulation.
source: Furthermore, at least for the TSHR and FSHR, expression levels in ependymal layer of the third ventricle was similar to that of the thyroid follicular cells and testicular Sertoli cells, respectively. Albeit intriguing, this may suggest a primary role for these receptors in central neural regulation.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the comparison of expression levels between brain and peripheral tissues.

claim: The ependymal layer of the third ventricle is juxtaposed to the anterior pituitary that produces TSH in response to hypothalamic TRH.
source: Among 173 Tshr-positive brain regions, subregions, and nuclei, the ependymal layer of the third ventricle displayed the highest Tshr transcript number and density. This region is juxtaposed to the anterior pituitary that produces TSH in response to hypothalamic TRH.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: TSH has been reported to be expressed in the hypothalamus.
source: Furthermore, TSH has been reported to be expressed in the hypothalamus (DeVito et al., 1986; Hojvat et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: A yet uncharacterized central TSH–TSHR feedback circuit may directly regulate the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis.
source: It is therefore possible that a yet uncharacterized central TSH–TSHR feedback circuit may directly regulate the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis, thought solely to be controlled by thyroid hormones.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the anatomical proximity and expression patterns.

claim: Thyroxine-to-triiodothyronine conversion occurs in tanycytes.
source: To add to this complexity, thyroxine-to-triiodothyronine conversion occurs in tanycytes (Fonseca et al., 2013), which calls into question whether central TSH actions regulate thyroid hormone metabolism in these cells and/or directly modulate hypothalamic TRH neuronal projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Central TSH actions may regulate thyroid hormone metabolism in tanycytes and/or directly modulate hypothalamic TRH neuronal projections.
source: To add to this complexity, thyroxine-to-triiodothyronine conversion occurs in tanycytes (Fonseca et al., 2013), which calls into question whether central TSH actions regulate thyroid hormone metabolism in these cells and/or directly modulate hypothalamic TRH neuronal projections.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the expression of TSHR in relevant brain regions.

claim: Tshr expression is not different between young and old mice.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that Tshr expression is not different between young and old mice (Kerp et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: There is conflicting evidence for the expression of TSH with age in rodents.
source: However, there is conflicting evidence for the expression of TSH with age—with evidence of no difference between 6-, 15-, and 22-month-old mice (Wang et al., 2019), but a 44% increase in the old rat compared with the young rat (Miler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work showing conflicting results.

claim: The nucleus of the horizontal limb of the diagonal band (HDB) of the forebrain is involved in learning.
source: The forebrain and olfactory bulb also displayed abundant Tshr transcripts, with the highest density in the nucleus of the horizontal limb of the diagonal band (HDB) of the forebrain and ventral tenia tecta (VTT) of the olfactory bulb. These regions are involved, respectively, in learning and odor processing (Shiotani et al., 2020; Cleland and Linster, 2019; McNamara et al., 2004; Chaves-Coira et al., 2018; Zhan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The ventral tenia tecta (VTT) of the olfactory bulb is involved in odor processing.
source: The forebrain and olfactory bulb also displayed abundant Tshr transcripts, with the highest density in the nucleus of the horizontal limb of the diagonal band (HDB) of the forebrain and ventral tenia tecta (VTT) of the olfactory bulb. These regions are involved, respectively, in learning and odor processing (Shiotani et al., 2020; Cleland and Linster, 2019; McNamara et al., 2004; Chaves-Coira et al., 2018; Zhan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The medial tuberal nucleus (MTu) of the hypothalamus controls ingestive behaviors and metabolism.
source: In the hypothalamus, the highest density was found in medial tuberal nucleus (MTu), which controls ingestive behaviors and metabolism (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Modulation of TSHRs in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) influences anxiety responses.
source: Finally, we found more recently that the modulation of TSHRs in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), which receives direct afferents from the MTu (Dong and Swanson, 2006), influences anxiety responses, suggesting that TSHR signaling might, in fact, mediate psychosocial behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data from the authors' recent work.

claim: The BNST receives direct afferents from the MTu.
source: Finally, we found more recently that the modulation of TSHRs in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), which receives direct afferents from the MTu (Dong and Swanson, 2006), influences anxiety responses, suggesting that TSHR signaling might, in fact, mediate psychosocial behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: TSHR signaling might mediate psychosocial behaviors.
source: Finally, we found more recently that the modulation of TSHRs in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), which receives direct afferents from the MTu (Dong and Swanson, 2006), influences anxiety responses, suggesting that TSHR signaling might, in fact, mediate psychosocial behaviors.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the observed effects of TSHR modulation on anxiety.

claim: The Lhcgr-rich mitral cell layer of the accessory olfactory bulb (MiA) has a known role in scent communication during mating.
source: The Lhcgr–rich mitral cell layer of the accessory olfactory bulb (MiA) has a known role in scent communication during mating (Gildersleeve et al., 2012; Lydell and Doty, 1972; Huck and Banks, 1984; Singh and Bronstad, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Men are attracted to cues of impending ovulation in women.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that men are attracted to cues of impending ovulation in women, raising an intriguing question on whether cycling hormones affect men's attraction and sexual behavior (Gildersleeve et al., 2012; Singh and Bronstad, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: LH surges in women during cycling may alter male sexual behavior through central mechanisms.
source: The broader question is whether LH surges in women during cycling may, in fact, alter male sexual behavior through central mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the expression of LHCGR in olfactory regions.

claim: The subfornical organ (SFO) sends efferent projections to the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT).
source: Second, a high Lhcgr density in the subfornical organ (SFO) of the forebrain was surprising. SFO sends efferent projections to the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT) (Miselis, 1981; Lind, 1986), which is surrounded by GnRH neurons and contains estrogen receptors (ESR) (Low, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The OVLT is surrounded by GnRH neurons and contains estrogen receptors (ESR).
source: Second, a high Lhcgr density in the subfornical organ (SFO) of the forebrain was surprising. SFO sends efferent projections to the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT) (Miselis, 1981; Lind, 1986), which is surrounded by GnRH neurons and contains estrogen receptors (ESR) (Low, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Circumventricular interactions between LHCGR, LH, GnRH, and ESR may underpin the central regulation of reproduction.
source: We therefore speculate that circumventricular interactions between LHCGR, LH, GnRH, and ESR underpin the central regulation of reproduction.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the anatomical connections and receptor expression patterns.

claim: The granular cell layer of the accessory olfactory bulb (GrA), granular layer of the dentate gyrus (GrDG), and agranular insular cortex (AIV) have known associations with odor processing, learning, memory formation, and anticipation of reward.
source: However, other Fshr-high subregions, including the granular cell layer of the accessory olfactory bulb (GrA), granular layer of the dentate gyrus (GrDG), and agranular insular cortex (AIV), have known associations with odor processing, learning, memory formation, and anticipation of reward (Eichenbaum, 2001; Nagayama et al., 2014; Kesner and Gilbert, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The anosmia of Kallman syndrome may arise from a dysfunctional FSHR-olfaction circuitry.
source: It is possible that the anosmia of Kallman syndrome, with unclear etiology, may arise from a dysfunctional FSHR-olfaction circuitry.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the expression of FSHR in olfactory regions.

claim: Inactivation of hippocampal Fshr blunts cognitive impairment and AD-like neuropathology induced by ovariectomy in 3xTg mice.
